newsitem.title: USA: Threat of fog postpones U.S. space shuttle landing.
newsitem.headline: Threat of fog postpones U.S. space shuttle landing.

text.p: The threat of fog forced NASA on Monday to postpone for one day the homecoming of the space shuttle Discovery after a jam-packed science mission.

The $2 billion reusable spaceship had been scheduled to return to Earth shortly after sunrise on Monday, but forecasters were concerned that the runway at the Kennedy Space Center would be obscured by fog.
"The probability of fog is too high to be acceptable," mission control's Dom Gorie told the astronauts moments before they were due to begin their descent.
The shuttle will make another landing attempt at 7:08 a.m. EDT (1108 GMT) on Tuesday, mission commentator Kyle Herring said.
The shuttle had only one landing slot on Monday because NASA officials passed on an earlier opportunity to avoid a more risky predawn touchdown.
Discovery's backup landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California was not considered on Monday because of the additional $900,000 cost of transporting the orbiter back to Florida.
The shuttle had enough fuel and supplies to stay aloft until Thursday, but would probably return to Earth on one coast or the other by Wednesday, flight director Wayne Hale had said earlier.

Discovery's crew of six, which includes a Canadian guest researcher, were to return with an atmospheric satellite carrying a bounty of information on the depletion of the Earth's protective ozone layer.
During the busy mission the astronauts tested a Japanese prototype space station robot arm, grew colon cancer cells for medical research, and pointed a telescope at the receding comet Hale-Bopp.

As Discovery's astronauts prepared to come home, the space shuttle Atlantis was being rolled to its seaside launch pad at the Kennedy Space Center for a planned late-September liftoff to Russia's Mir space station.
